summary: This document describes the style conventions and editorial policies the RFC Editor uses for the RFC Series. It covers how an RFC should be structured and written, and points to a website with extra, more experimental guidance. It replaces earlier style guidance.

plainLanguage.summary: An RFC is a technical document with a standard shape and a standard voice. This memo is the rulebook the editors follow: which parts every document must have and in what order, how sentences and lists are punctuated, when to use capitals, how to name and cite other documents, and how the boilerplate at the front and back is filled in. It keeps a large, many-author series looking like one series.

subtitle: The house style for RFCs: how they are structured, punctuated, capitalized and referenced before the RFC Editor publishes them.

tldr.problem: RFCs come from many sources and authors, so without a shared set of rules the document series would not look or read consistently, and references, status notes and boilerplate would vary from document to document.
tldr.mechanism: This memo lays out the required structure of an RFC, from the first-page header to the author's address, and then gives the RFC Editor's conventions for language, punctuation, capitalization, citations, figures, references and copyright.
tldr.outcome: It is the current Informational style guide: it obsoletes RFC 2223 and has been updated by RFC 7997.

today: RFC 7322 is an Informational RFC published in September 2014. It obsoletes RFC 2223 and has been updated by RFC 7997, which extended its coverage of non-ASCII characters. It describes the style the RFC Editor applies to documents in every stream.

sections.title: Purpose of the Style Guide
sections.content:
This document describes the editorial style of the RFC Series. It is written for authors, editors and others who contribute to RFCs, and it explains the conventions the RFC Editor applies. Editing is not an additional technical review: where the RFC Editor suggests wording for clarity, it is the author, working group or stream-approving body that decides whether the change affects the technical meaning, and original wording that is more accurate takes precedence over editorial convention. The RFC Editor calls the tension between author and editor "editorial balance."

There is a prime directive above all grammatical convention: do not change the intended meaning of the text. If a document cannot be edited without serious risk of changing its meaning, it may be returned to the stream-approving body for review.

The guide uses lowercase "must" and "should" in a special way that differs from the requirement-level keywords of RFC 2119. Lowercase "must" marks changes the RFC Editor applies automatically and that are not at the author's discretion; lowercase "should" marks recommended usage that the editor may question but that is not required.
sections.plainLanguage: The editor's job is to make documents clear and consistent, never to change what they mean. When a change might affect the technical content, the authors decide. The words must and should are used here in an everyday sense, not in the strict sense that standards documents give them.

sections.title: The Shape of an RFC
sections.content:
A published RFC largely contains a defined list of elements. The first-page header, the title, the abstract, the body and the author's address are required, and so are the Security Considerations section and, for Internet-Drafts, the IANA Considerations section. Other parts, such as the RFC Editor or stream note, the Status of This Memo section, the copyright notice and the table of contents, are supplied by the RFC Editor. Sections marked for the editor are added during the editorial process when necessary.

The strongly recommended order runs from the first-page header and title through the abstract, status, copyright and table of contents, then the body, which starts with an Introduction and a Requirements Language section and can include IANA Considerations, Internationalization Considerations and Security Considerations before the references and appendices. The References section is split into normative and informative subsections. Within the body this order is strongly recommended and exceptions may be questioned; outside the body the order is required. Sections are allowed to contain nothing but subsections.

Elements before the body of the memo are not numbered. Typically the body uses numbered sections and the appendices use letters, and anything after the appendices is neither numbered nor labeled.
sections.plainLanguage: Every RFC has a fixed skeleton: a header, a title, a short abstract, status and copyright notes, a table of contents, the numbered body, references and appendices, and finally the author's address. Some parts the authors write and some the editor fills in, and the order of the parts outside the body is fixed.

sections.title: Language and Punctuation
sections.content:
The publication language is English. Spelling may be American or British so long as an individual document is internally consistent; where both are used in one document or a cluster of documents, the text is made consistent with American English spelling. Capitalization must be consistent within a document and ideally with related RFCs, the major words in titles use title case except for internal articles, prepositions and conjunctions, and section titles that are sentences use sentence capitalization.

Punctuation rules are specific. There is no overstriking or underlining, and when a sentence ended by a period is followed by another sentence there must be two blank spaces after the period. A comma is used before the last item of a series. When literal text is quoted, punctuation goes outside the quotation marks; when general text is quoted, punctuation may go inside. Quotation marks are not needed for a block quotation.

Names and URLs have their own conventions. DNS names used as generic examples should come from the reserved example set so they cannot collide with real names, and angle brackets are strongly recommended around URLs. Abbreviations should be expanded early except for well-known ones, the online abbreviation list is not exhaustive or definitive, and some terms that look like abbreviations are fixed names that should not be expanded.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules are about consistency: pick one spelling style and stay with it, capitalize titles in the usual way, put two spaces after a full stop that ends a sentence, use a comma before the last item in a list, and use the reserved example names when giving examples so no real site is accidentally named.

sections.title: Citations and References
sections.content:
Citations and references must match: there must be a reference for every citation and a citation for every reference. Citations are enclosed in square brackets, and a citation or reference tag must not contain spaces, so the tag is RFC2119 rather than RFC 2119; the ordinary textual naming of an RFC, as in "See RFC 2119", does contain a space. Ranges are written with a single hyphen and no spaces, as in [RFC2119]-[RFC2120], and multiple citations are separated by commas.

Cross-references inside a document and to other RFCs use section numbers rather than page numbers, because pagination can change from one format or device to another. The References section is divided into normative references, which a reader must understand to implement or interpret the document, and informative references, which are background. RFC Editor conventions govern how the entries themselves are formatted and how much the editor may adjust them.
sections.plainLanguage: Every mention of another document must have a matching entry in the reference list and the other way around. The bracketed labels carry no spaces, and the proper name of a document, like RFC 2119, does have one. Point readers at sections, not page numbers, because pages move when a document is reformatted.

sections.title: Security, IANA and the Rest
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section is required. The RFC Editor expects authors to give serious consideration to security and may ask for more when a section seems thin, referring authors to the guidelines for writing RFC text on security considerations. Documents that define a protocol, a data format or a management structure are expected to discuss the security implications rather than simply state that there are none.

IANA Considerations is required in an Internet-Draft, where registration actions and registry assignments must be described. The guide also covers the abstract, the status of this memo, the copyright notice, the table of contents, figures and tables, the author's address, and the handling of informal and non-ASCII characters.

These conventions are lubricants for a diverse series, not a technical review. The guide itself states that it has no security considerations of its own, which is fitting for a document about editing rather than protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: Two sections are mandatory for the right reasons: every document must discuss security, and drafts must explain any registry entries they ask for. The rest of the guide covers the smaller pieces, such as the abstract, the table of contents, figures and the author's address.
